Canvas Assignment Bodies

How to paste one of these

One assignment per topic, the graded companion to its calendar event. Built from the same schedule and lesson data, so the two cannot disagree.

  1. Canvas, Assignments, the assignment for this topic, Edit.
  2. In the Rich Content Editor click the </> icon to open the HTML editor. Never paste into the visual editor.
  3. Press Copy HTML and paste the whole block.
  4. In Assign to, add one row per section from the table, remove the Everyone row, and save.
  5. The assignment name is yours to type: identical in Canvas and PowerSchool, plain ASCII.

AP World History · Unit 1: The Global Tapestry
Topic 1.5: State Building in Africa
GGreen DayTuesday, September 8 SSilver DayWednesday, September 9

OVERVIEW

African states in this period were built on connection, not isolation. Mali and the Hausa city-states sat on the trans-Saharan routes, the Swahili coast on the Indian Ocean monsoon, Great Zimbabwe on gold moving toward that coast, and Ethiopia on a Christianity older than most of Europe's. This assignment asks you to learn how each used trade, religion, and architecture to build authority, and you meet a case where the archaeology itself was pressured to produce a politically convenient answer about who built Great Zimbabwe.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 01 Map & Geography Check. Where African states sat relative to trade routes, and why that geography helped decide which ones grew powerful.
  • 02 First & 10 Reading. The Weight of the Walls, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Causation in African state building.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. State power: trade, religion, and architecture.
  • 08 Primary Source. Ibn Battuta on African governance, from his 1352 visit to Mali.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. AP argument: two examples, change, causation.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. Walls That Spoke for Kings.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Compare evidence from at least TWO African states. Separate observation from inference: first identify what the object, building, or map actually shows; then explain what it suggests about labor, trade, religion, geography, or political authority. Do not assume every African state built power in the same way.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Enter the Great Zimbabwe court. Choose your role, king, gold trader, Swahili merchant, or regional chief, and advise the court on how to maintain power in a changing world.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how and why states in Africa developed and changed from c. 1200 to c. 1450.
  • I can describe how trade, religion, and geography shaped state power in Great Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, and the Hausa kingdoms.
  • I can explain how Islam and Christianity functioned as tools of governance, not just belief, in African states.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can use specific evidence about Great Zimbabwe's stone enclosures, gold trade, and Indian Ocean connections to explain how it built power.
  • I can explain how Ethiopia's Solomonic dynasty used Christianity and control of Red Sea trade to maintain independence and legitimacy.
  • I can describe how Hausa city-states used trans-Saharan trade and Islamic administration to build and exercise power.

HOW TO SUBMIT
  1. Work the six modules above in BeHistorical. Typing saves on this computer only, and saving is not submitting. Your drafts do not follow you to another Chromebook and your teacher cannot see them.
  2. Scroll to the Save Your Work panel, below the module cards.
  3. Click Gather All My Work, then Copy to Clipboard.
  4. Come back here, paste into the text box, and submit.

The First & 10 answers are the fragile ones. The reading opens in its own window, so if you never open it, those three slots come through blank.

AP World History · Unit 1: The Global Tapestry
Topic 1.6: Developments in Europe
GGreen DayThursday, September 10 SSilver DayFriday, September 11

OVERVIEW

Europe is this period's case of a region that did not centralize, and the useful question is what grew in the space where a large state did not. A Church with its own courts, its own revenue, and the power to excommunicate a king. Chartered towns that bought their independence. Guilds. Assemblies that traded money for a say in how it was spent. This assignment asks you to follow all four, and then the plague, which did more to end serfdom than any monarch managed.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. The Edge of the World, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Comparison with Song China.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Feudalism and fragmentation.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Enter a feudal manor in crisis and debate how it should respond to the Black Death. Your final step out of character reflection is the part that is collected.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. Christianity, towns, and change.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. A Calendar of Labor.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO cards from different categories: political relationships, Church authority, or labor/economic life. For each, record one detail you can actually see before making an inference. Some evidence predates c. 1200; when it does, use it as a continuity baseline rather than pretending it documents the entire period.
  • 08 Primary Source. Bishop Fulbert of Chartres on the Duties of a Vassal.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how European political structures developed in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450.
  • I can describe how Christianity, feudalism, manorialism, and cities shaped European society.
  • I can explain how Europe compared with other regions of Unit 1 in state power, belief systems, and economic organization.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can use evidence about monarchies, nobles, the Church, and decentralized power to explain European politics.
  • I can explain the roles of feudalism, manorialism, towns, guilds, and trade in European society.
  • I can compare Europe with Song China, Dar al-Islam, Africa, the Americas, or South and Southeast Asia.

AP World History · Unit 1: The Global Tapestry
Topic 1.7: Comparison in the Period from c. 1200 to c. 1450
GGreen DayMonday, September 14 SSilver DayTuesday, September 15

OVERVIEW

This topic adds no new content and one new skill. You already have six regions; today you lay them side by side under one question at a time, how each extracted resources, how each justified its rule, how each ordered its society. Then you learn what a comparison sentence has to contain before it earns anything. Two facts about two places is not a comparison. A claim, the specific evidence underneath it, and the reason the difference existed is.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. A World of Different Answers, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Build a Unit 1 Comparison.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Build a comparison.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO evidence cards from different regions that can be compared through the SAME category: administration, legitimacy, labor, trade, or political organization. First record one concrete detail from each card. Then infer what each detail suggests before deciding whether the pattern is similar or different.
  • 09 Checkpoint 2. Write a comparison paragraph.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. “Similar” Does Not Mean “Same”.
  • 08 Primary Source. Marco Polo Compares Hangzhou to the Cities He Knew.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can compare methods of state building across regions from c. 1200 to c. 1450.
  • I can compare how belief systems shaped politics and society across Unit 1 regions.
  • I can write a clear AP-style comparison using specific evidence from at least two regions.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can identify one meaningful similarity and one meaningful difference between two Unit 1 regions.
  • I can support each comparison with specific evidence such as Song bureaucracy, Dar al-Islam scholarship, Mali trade, Inca roads, or European feudalism.
  • I can explain why the similarity or difference existed instead of only naming it.

AP World History · Unit 2: Networks of Exchange
Topic 2.1: The Silk Roads
GGreen DayWednesday, September 16 SSilver DayThursday, September 17

OVERVIEW

Long-distance Silk Roads trade expanded after 1200 because rising demand for luxury goods made the journey worth financing while caravanserais, credit, banking houses, paper money, and periods of relative political stability reduced merchant risk and cost. Today you follow that economic chain from demand to easier exchange to the growth of trading cities such as Kashgar and Samarkand, then to producers in China, Persia, and India expanding output for distant markets.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 01 Map & Geography Check. The overland routes, relay stations, and pastoral intermediaries that made Silk Road trade possible.
  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: Why Silk Roads Trade Expanded, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Demand, caravanserais, credit, banking, money economies, and supporting political stability.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. Trading cities and production respond to expanding exchange.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. Carry Trust Instead of Coins.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Explain the Silk Roads Growth Chain.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Use the cards as evidence, not as answers. Choose TWO cards. For each, identify a visible or concrete feature, infer what it suggests about exchange, and state what the source cannot establish by itself. Then connect the two pieces to one historical claim.
  • 08 Primary Source. Marco Polo on Money and Exchange.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Become a Silk Road merchant and decide how credit, caravanserais, political protection, and market demand shape a long-distance trading journey.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain why Silk Roads trade expanded after 1200 by connecting demand, commercial practices, transportation infrastructure, and supporting political stability.
  • I can explain how caravanserai, credit, banking houses, and paper money reduced the risk and difficulty of long-distance trade.
  • I can explain how demand for luxury goods increased production and helped trading cities such as Kashgar and Samarkand grow.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can build a cause-and-effect chain: demand plus improved trade systems and lower political risk increased trade volume and geographic reach.
  • I can explain what caravanserai, bills of exchange, banking houses, and paper money actually did for merchants instead of only defining the terms.
  • I can use Kashgar, Samarkand, Chinese porcelain, Persian and Indian textiles, and Chinese iron and steel as evidence of economic change.

HOW TO SUBMIT
  1. Work the four modules above in BeHistorical. Typing saves on this computer only, and saving is not submitting. Your drafts do not follow you to another Chromebook and your teacher cannot see them.
  2. Scroll to the Save Your Work panel, below the module cards.
  3. Click Gather All My Work, then Copy to Clipboard.
  4. Come back here, paste into the text box, and submit.

AP World History · Unit 2: Networks of Exchange
Topic 2.2: The Mongol Empire
GGreen DayFriday, September 18 SSilver DayMonday, September 21

OVERVIEW

The Mongols first built an enormous Eurasian empire, then divided it into khanates, but their expansion still reshaped exchange across the continent. Today you follow how Mongol rule facilitated trade and communication and how intensified contact transferred knowledge and practices across regions, including Greco-Islamic medical knowledge toward western Europe, numbering systems into Europe, and the adoption of the Uyghur script by the Mongols.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 01 Map & Geography Check. How far the Mongol Empire and its four khanates stretched, and why that reach mattered for trade.
  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: Build, Connect, Transfer, Fragment, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. What Changed Under Mongol Rule?
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Conquest, administration, khanates, and fragmentation.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Enter a Mongol court and weigh the administrative, commercial, and cultural consequences of ruling a connected Eurasian empire.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. Pax Mongolica, communication, and cultural/technological transfer.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. An Empire That Borrowed to Rule.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Use TWO evidence cards to test what Mongol rule changed. Distinguish political control from the movement of merchants, specialists, knowledge, and technologies.
  • 08 Primary Source. William of Rubruck on Mongol Administration and Connectivity.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how the Mongols built a vast Eurasian empire and why that empire fragmented into regional khanates over time.
  • I can explain how Mongol expansion facilitated Afro-Eurasian trade and communication without treating the Silk Roads as a new Mongol invention.
  • I can explain how Mongol-era interregional contact encouraged technological and cultural transfers across Eurasia.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can connect Mongol military organization and adaptation to conquest, then connect succession, distance, and regional interests to fragmentation into the Yuan, Ilkhanate, Chagatai Khanate, and Golden Horde.
  • I can explain how merchant protection, reduced political barriers, and the Yam relay system improved trade and communication across Mongol-controlled Eurasia.
  • I can use Greco-Islamic medical knowledge, numbering systems, and the adoption of the Uyghur script as evidence of cultural and technological transfer.

AP World History · Unit 2: Networks of Exchange
Topic 2.3: Exchange in the Indian Ocean
GGreen DayTuesday, September 22 SSilver DayWednesday, September 23

OVERVIEW

Indian Ocean exchange expanded because merchants learned to use predictable monsoon winds and improved maritime technologies such as the compass, astrolabe, and larger ship designs. Today you follow how that expanding system strengthened trading states and cities including the Swahili Coast, Gujarat, and Malacca, created diasporic merchant communities, and connected regions strongly enough for voyages such as Zheng He's to operate across an already mature network.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 01 Map & Geography Check. The monsoon winds and port cities that turned the Indian Ocean into a highway rather than a barrier.
  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: The Ocean That Ran on a Schedule, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Monsoons, compass, astrolabe, and larger ships.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Question: After 1200, how much did knowledge of the environment, especially monsoon winds, help Indian Ocean trade grow compared with the power of states?
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Enter an Indian Ocean port and make decisions shaped by monsoon timing, merchant diasporas, port-state politics, and long-distance exchange.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. State growth, merchant communities, and interregional contact.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. A Schedule Written by the Wind.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Explain Why Indian Ocean Trade Intensified.
  • 08 Primary Source. Ibn Battuta on Kilwa.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how monsoon knowledge, the compass, astrolabe, and larger ship designs helped Indian Ocean trade expand after 1200.
  • I can explain how expanded Indian Ocean trade promoted powerful trading cities and states such as the Swahili Coast city-states, Gujarat, and the Sultanate of Malacca.
  • I can explain how diasporic merchant communities and Zheng He's voyages demonstrate the cultural and technological effects of intensified Indian Ocean exchange.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain how predictable monsoon winds and navigational or shipbuilding innovations lowered the risk and increased the range of maritime trade.
  • I can use the Swahili Coast, Gujarat, and Malacca to explain how trade fostered state growth and powerful commercial centers.
  • I can use Arab and Persian communities in East Africa, Chinese merchant communities in Southeast Asia, Malay communities in the Indian Ocean basin, and Zheng He as evidence of cross-cultural interaction.

Topic 2.4: Trans-Saharan Trade Routes
GGreen DayThursday, September 24 SSilver DayFriday, September 25

OVERVIEW

Trans-Saharan trade grew because camel technology and organized caravans made regular long-distance movement across the desert possible. Today you follow how complementary demand for goods such as gold and salt increased the volume and geographic range of exchange and how Mali used its position in that network to facilitate trade, collect wealth, and project power across West Africa.

AP World History · Unit 2: Networks of Exchange
Topic 2.5: Cultural Consequences of Connectivity
GGreen DayMonday, September 28 SSilver DayTuesday, September 29

OVERVIEW

Expanded exchange networks changed culture as well as commerce. Today you follow three connected consequences: religions, artistic traditions, and technologies such as paper and gunpowder diffused across regions; the fortunes of cities rose or fell with changing patterns of trade and urbanization; and a more connected Afro-Eurasia produced more written travel accounts from observers such as Ibn Battuta, Marco Polo, and Margery Kempe.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: Goods Were Never the Only Cargo, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Religion, paper, and gunpowder across Afro-Eurasia.
  • 08 Primary Source. Ibn Battuta Describes the Port of Zaytun (Quanzhou).
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. Urban fortunes and written travel accounts.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. The Medieval World Through Travelers' Eyes.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Track a Cultural Consequence of Connectivity.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO cards that illuminate different consequences of connectivity: cultural/technological diffusion, urban change, or travel writing.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Travel through a connected intellectual world and decide what knowledge to preserve, translate, carry, and record for audiences far from where you encountered it.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how expanding exchange networks spread cultural traditions and technological innovations across Afro-Eurasia.
  • I can explain why expanding trade networks produced both increased urbanization and periods of decline in connected cities.
  • I can explain why intensified exchange produced more written travel accounts and use Ibn Battuta, Margery Kempe, and Marco Polo as evidence.

  • I can use Ibn Battuta, Margery Kempe, and Marco Polo to show how intensified connectivity increased travel and the written record of cross-cultural encounters.

OVERVIEW

A few empires got huge after 1450, and guns are a big part of why. Today you follow the story: cannons broke the walls that had protected castles and cities, only big states with big treasuries could afford them, and the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, and Qing empires grew. Then you see what happened when growing empires ran into each other, through the Safavid and Mughal rivalry and Morocco's war with Songhai.

Start with what the source directly shows, then infer what it suggests about military technology, geographic expansion, or imperial power. A map or portrait can show scale or political memory, but it cannot prove a causal mechanism by itself.

OVERVIEW

Gunpowder won these empires their land, but holding it was the hard part. Today you follow the three jobs every ruler had to do: find people who would serve him, convince everyone he deserved to rule, and collect the money to pay for it all. You compare how different rulers did the same job, from the Ottoman devshirme and Japan's salaried samurai to Versailles and Mughal tombs, and explain why they did it differently.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: Holding What You Won, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Compare two ways rulers built officials and soldiers who depended on them.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO cards from different empires. For each, decide which job it is evidence for: people who serve, symbols that justify, or the size of the problem rulers faced. Start with what the source directly shows, then infer what it suggests. A painting, a building or a map can show how a ruler wanted to be seen or how big his empire was; it cannot by itself show how taxes were collected or whether officials stayed loyal.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Serve on Akbar’s administrative commission at Fatehpur Sikri and decide how to rank officers, assess revenue, and assign jagirs without creating independent provincial powers. Your final Step out of the room reflection is the part that is collected.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. How rulers made their power look rightful, and how they paid for it.

Topic 4.1: Technological Innovations

OVERVIEW

Unit 3 was about empires that grew on land. Unit 4 begins at sea, with a problem: in the 1400s, sailing south along the coast of West Africa was the easy part, because the wind and the current fought every ship that tried to come back. Today you follow how sailors solved it. Europe borrowed tools from older worlds, the compass from China, the astrolabe and tables of the sky from Greek and Islamic astronomers, and the lateen sail from the Mediterranean, built new ships around them, and learned to ride the Atlantic's winds home. For each piece, explain where it came from and what it let sailors do.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

Topic 4.2: Exploration: Causes and Events

OVERVIEW

Last class, ships learned to cross the ocean and come home. Today you find out who paid for those voyages and what they got for it. Follow three groups of states, Portugal around Africa, Spain to the west, and England, France, and the Dutch to the north, and for each one explain who paid, what they wanted, and what the voyages actually produced.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: Who Paid?, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Why rulers backed ocean voyages, and how: by paying, or by granting rights.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Advise Isabella and Ferdinand at Santa Fe in 1492: decide whether to pay for Columbus's voyage west, what to promise him, and what to do about Portugal's claims.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. One Portuguese or Spanish voyage, one English, French, or Dutch voyage: who paid, why, and what it produced.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. You Are a Sailor on Columbus's Fleet, October 11, 1492.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Making Connections: How One State's Voyage Led to Another's.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO cards. For each, say what kind of source it is (a monument, a later picture, a map made at the time, or a modern map), what it directly shows, and what it suggests about who paid for exploration or what the voyages produced.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can describe the role of states in maritime exploration: how rulers backed voyages, by paying for them or by granting explorers rights, and what they offered explorers in return.
  • I can explain why Portugal and Spain backed voyages and what they got: Portugal's ships and navigation led it around Africa to a trading-post empire, and Spain's voyages across the Atlantic and Pacific made all of Europe more interested in ocean trade.
  • I can explain why England, France, and the Dutch sponsored northern Atlantic crossings, and what those voyages produced instead of a route to Asia.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain one economic reason rulers backed voyages (such as cutting out the middlemen in the spice trade) and name one thing a ruler gave an explorer (such as ships, permission to claim land, titles, or a share of the profits).
  • For a Portuguese or Spanish voyage, I can name who backed it, what they wanted, and one economic effect, such as Portugal's trading-post empire or Spain's voyages making Europe more interested in ocean trade.
  • I can use one English, French, or Dutch voyage to explain the search for another route to Asia and one effect it had, such as cod fishing, the fur trade, or land claims, and explain how Portugal's and Spain's hold on the southern routes led that state to look north.

Topic 4.3: Columbian Exchange
GGreen DayTuesday, November 3 SSilver DayWednesday, November 4

OVERVIEW

Last class, rulers paid for ships to cross the ocean. Today you find out what else those ships carried. Some things crossed on purpose, like horses, cattle, and wheat, some crossed by accident, like smallpox and the rats in the cargo, and some crossed with enslaved Africans carried by force. For each one, explain how it crossed and what it did to the people at the other end, in the Americas and in Africa, Asia, and Europe.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: What the Ships Carried, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Claims and Evidence: What Did the Writer Use to Prove It?
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Why diseases from the Eastern Hemisphere were so deadly in the Americas.
  • 08 Primary Source. A Nahua Account of Smallpox in Tenochtitlan, 1520.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. The cause of the Columbian Exchange, and one effect in each hemisphere.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. You Are a Healer in Tenochtitlan, Autumn 1520.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO cards: one about something that crossed to the Americas (the Florentine Codex or the sugar plantation) and one about American crops in Afro-Eurasia (the English herbal or the Qing album). The Andes harvest, drawn in 1615, shows maize and potatoes grown in the Americas, where both were farmed long before 1492; use it as background. The English herbal shows a crop arriving and being named, so pair it with a claim about the crops spreading; the Qing album shows people relying on one.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Sit on a town council in the Valley of Mexico in 1531, eleven years after smallpox: decide what to plant, what to do about the settlers' animals, and how to care for the sick when a new sickness arrives.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain what caused the Columbian Exchange: ships crossing the Atlantic, and later the Pacific, and coming back, carrying plants, animals, and germs, some on purpose and some by accident.
  • I can explain how diseases from the Eastern Hemisphere, such as smallpox, measles, and malaria, and disease vectors, such as rats and mosquitoes, crossed to the Americas, and why these diseases had catastrophic effects on many Indigenous populations.
  • I can explain the effects of the exchange on both hemispheres. In the Americas: animals and crops Europeans brought, foods enslaved Africans brought, and cash crops grown on plantations with coerced labor. In Afro-Eurasia: American staple crops that improved nutrition.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can state the cause of the Columbian Exchange and give one thing that crossed on purpose and one that crossed by accident.
  • I can name a disease and a disease vector, and give two reasons these diseases were so deadly in the Americas, including one about the conditions people lived in, such as war, forced labor, or hunger.
  • I can explain one effect in the Americas and one in Afro-Eurasia, each with a specific animal, crop, or food and the people it affected.

OVERVIEW

Last class ended with a question: who would do the work in the new colonies, and who would rule? Today you find out, and the answer reaches Africa and Asia too. Rival European states built forts on the coasts and colonies in the Americas, but China and Japan set their own terms, Asian merchants kept trading, and Kongo and Asante grew stronger. For each case, explain what changed and what kept going, in who ruled, in work, and in slavery.

LEARNING TARGETS

SUCCESS CRITERIA

  • I can explain one continuity in who set the terms of trade: how China or Japan kept control of trade with Europeans, or how a merchant group such as Gujaratis, Swahili Arabs, Omanis, or Javanese kept Indian Ocean trade going even after the Portuguese began forcing ships to buy the cartaz.
  • I can explain one labor system that continued in a new form and one that was new, and how each supplied workers for farms or mines.

Topic 4.5: Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed
GGreen DayMonday, November 9 SSilver DayTuesday, November 10

OVERVIEW

Last class, Europeans built empires from the sea. Today you find out how rulers made those empires pay. Follow the tools they built, mercantilist laws and companies that could go to war, then follow what those tools moved: silver pulled all the way to China, goods and enslaved people across the Atlantic, and more work for ordinary spinners and weavers. For each part, explain what was new and what kept going, then explain what the trade did to families in Africa and compare how religions spread, clashed and blended.

  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Sit on Manila's council in 1594 and decide how to keep the silver-for-silk trade paying for the colony, when the king of Spain wants to limit it, Chinese merchants run it, and rivals want to take it.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. What the slave trade did to families in Africa, how Atlantic cultures mixed, and how religions spread, clashed, and blended.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how European rulers used mercantilism and chartered joint-stock companies to make their empires pay and to compete with each other, and how economic disputes led to rivalries and wars.
  • I can explain what changed and what continued in networks of exchange from 1450 to 1750: silver pulled toward China, the Atlantic trading system, regional markets that kept flourishing, and peasant and artisan work that continued and grew.
  • I can explain how the trade in enslaved people changed families and communities in parts of Africa, and how Africans, Indigenous Americans, and Europeans all contributed to new mixed cultures in the Atlantic world.
  • I can compare how religions affected societies as contact grew: how existing religions spread, how contact caused religious conflict, and how new blended, or syncretic, beliefs and practices developed.

SUCCESS CRITERIA

  • I can use two examples to compare how religions spread, clashed, or blended, and say one way they were similar and one way they were different.

Topic 4.6: Internal and External Challenges to State Power
GGreen DayWednesday, November 11 SSilver DayThursday, November 12

OVERVIEW

Last class, rulers built tools to make their empires pay, and they reached further than ever. Today you find out who pushed back. Judges and nobles in France, peasants and Cossacks in Russia, a warrior kingdom in India, a queen in Africa, and Pueblo towns in New Mexico all resisted a state that was pushing on them, and enslaved people in Brazil, Jamaica and South Carolina organized to challenge the colonies that held them. For each case, explain what the state pushed for, who pushed back and how, and what happened next.

Topic 4.7: Changing Social Hierarchies

OVERVIEW

Last class, you saw people push back against growing states. Today you find out who ended up where. Every society still ranked people from top to bottom, but empires changed who stood on which rung: the Ottomans took in Jewish refugees that Spain pushed out, the Mughal emperor Akbar welcomed Hindu princes into his army, the Manchus conquered China and built a new elite, the casta system put Spanish-born officials at the top in the Americas, and stronger rulers squeezed old nobles in the Ottoman Empire, Russia, and France. OVERVIEW

Last class ended with a question: trade, work, and the social ladder all moved between 1450 and 1750, so which change mattered most, and what stayed the same? Today you answer it with an argument. Follow the new trade in sugar, silver, and cloth all the way to the people: the workers it needed, the society of masters and slaves it built on Barbados, and the villages it changed in Africa. Then name what stayed the same, connect your evidence, and write a thesis.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: Follow the Trade to the People, plus all three check questions inside the reading.

  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Follow one economic development to the workers it needed and to one change in a social structure.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO cards: one that shows a change in a social structure (who was forced to work, who rose, how families lived), and one that shows something that stayed the same.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. A thesis and a short argument: how economic developments changed social structures, and what stayed the same.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER

  • 03 Content Delivery.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how economic developments between 1450 and 1750, such as the new demand for sugar, silver, and cloth, increased the demand for workers, and how that demand was met.
  • I can explain how those economic developments changed social structures: who was forced to work, who rose to the top, and how families lived, in places such as Barbados, Spanish America, and West Central Africa.
  • I can write a thesis and a short argument about how much social structures changed between 1450 and 1750, and what stayed the same, connecting evidence from different Unit 4 topics.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can follow one economic development (plantation sugar, Potosí silver, or the demand for cloth) to the workers it needed.
  • I can explain one change that development made to a social structure, such as slavery for life in Barbados, the casta ranking, or villages in West Central Africa with more women than men.
  • I can write a thesis that names one change and one continuity, support it with evidence from at least three Unit 4 topics, and explain how two pieces of my evidence relate.

AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions
Topic 5.1: The Enlightenment
GGreen DayMonday, November 30 SSilver DayTuesday, December 1

OVERVIEW

Last unit ended with a question: by 1750 the oceans were joined and states were stronger than ever, so who do those states belong to? Today you meet the writers who asked every king, church, and noble the same question: by what right? You will learn their new answers, natural rights, the social contract, and religious toleration, see how the ideas spread before the Atlantic revolutions, and follow them into the 1800s, as reformers ended slavery and serfdom, widened the vote, and women demanded equal rights. Then you decide how much had really changed by 1900.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: By What Right?, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Find the Claim.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. One new Enlightenment idea, the old answer it challenged, how the ideas spread before the Atlantic revolutions, and how the people became the nation.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. One reform movement, what drove it, how far it got by 1900, and what had still not changed.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. Seneca Falls, New York, July 20, 1848.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose TWO cards. For each, decide what claim the source makes or what it shows about Enlightenment ideas and their effects. An object can make a claim too, without a single sentence of argument.
  • 08 Primary Source. The Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls, 1848.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Paris, 1788 to 1789. A publisher must decide what a pamphlet on natural rights will claim, whose voices it will print, and who will get to read it, when the people paying for it, the writers, and the people the words leave out all want different things.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain the new way of thinking Enlightenment writers used to question where rulers got their power, and at least one of their new ideas: natural rights, the social contract, or religious toleration.
  • I can explain how Enlightenment ideas spread and came before the revolutions in the Atlantic world, and how the idea that a state belongs to its people became loyalty to the nation.
  • I can explain how reform movements, pushed by Enlightenment ideas, religious faith, and other causes, ended slavery and serfdom, widened the vote, and demanded women's rights between 1750 and 1900, and what had still not changed by 1900.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain one new Enlightenment idea (natural rights, the social contract, or religious toleration), name a writer who argued it (Locke, Rousseau, or Voltaire), and explain how it challenged the old answer that rulers' power came from God, tradition, and birth.
  • I can explain one way Enlightenment ideas spread (books such as the Encyclopédie, salons, coffeehouses, or letters), explain what it means that the ideas came before the revolutions that began in 1775, 1789, 1791, and 1810, and explain how "the people" came to mean the nation.
  • I can choose one reform movement (abolition, the end of serfdom, the right to vote, or women's rights), explain what pushed it forward (Enlightenment ideas, religious faith, or another cause) with one piece of evidence (such as the 1787 antislavery society, Russia in 1861, Olympe de Gouges, Mary Wollstonecraft, or Seneca Falls), and name what it had changed by 1900 and one thing that had not.

AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions
Topic 5.2: Nationalism and Revolutions
GGreen DayWednesday, December 2 SSilver DayThursday, December 3

OVERVIEW

By 1789 the new ideas about rights were everywhere educated people read, but ideas alone never overthrew a king. Today you find out what else it took: a grievance, the words to name it, and a chance to act, in America, France, Haiti, and Spanish America, and you see how each revolution helped another one start or win. Then you follow what they left behind, new countries, new ideas about government, and a new loyalty to the nation that joined Italy and Germany together and broke the Balkans away from the Ottoman Empire.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: How Revolutions Made Nations, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Compare Two Sources.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. One revolution's grievance, words, and chance, what it created, and how it was linked to another revolution.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. What a nation is, how governments used shared loyalty, one country nationalism joined together, and one people it pulled away from an empire.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. Les Cayes, Haiti, March 1816.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose at least two evidence cards. For each, say what kind of source it is and who made it, name one precise detail rather than summarizing it, explain what that detail shows about a cause or an effect of the revolutions, and name one thing the source cannot tell you. The caption identifies the source; it does not supply your conclusion.
  • 08 Primary Source. Simón Bolívar, the Letter from Jamaica, 1815.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Port-Républicain (Port-au-Prince), Saint-Domingue, spring 1801. The revolution has ended slavery in the colony, and France still claims it. A council must write a constitution that protects that freedom, keeps people fed and the colony defended, and decides how far to stand against France.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how a grievance, the words of a revolutionary document, and a chance to act came together to cause revolutions against kings and empires between 1750 and 1900.
  • I can explain what the American, French, Haitian, and Spanish American revolutions created, including independent states in the Americas and new ideas about government such as liberalism and democracy, and how each revolution helped another one start or win.
  • I can explain how a new loyalty to the nation, built on a shared language, religion, customs, and homeland, was used by governments and by nationalists to join some states together and to pull peoples away from empires.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can choose one revolution (American, French, Haitian, or Spanish American) and name its grievance (such as British taxes, noble privilege and bread prices, slavery, or creoles shut out of high office), its words (America: the Declaration of Independence; France: the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen; Haiti: that French declaration as free people of color claimed it, or Toussaint Louverture's proclamation of 1793; Spanish America: Bolívar's Letter from Jamaica, written five years into the fighting), and its chance (such as Britain's distance, a bankrupt king, a France in revolution, or Napoleon's invasion of Spain).
  • I can name what one revolution created (such as the United States, a republic under its 1787 Constitution, Haiti in 1804, or the independent countries of Spanish America by 1826), explain one link in the chain (such as France's debt from the American war, or Haiti's help to Bolívar in 1816), and explain liberalism or democracy as a new idea about government.
  • I can explain what a nation is (people who share a language, a religion, customs, and a homeland), give one example of a government using national loyalty (revolutionary France in 1793) or building a shared loyalty to hold back nationalism (Ottomanism), and give one example of nationalism joining states (Italy in 1861 or Germany in 1871) and one of it pulling a people away from an empire (Greece in 1830, or Serbia, Montenegro, or Romania in 1878).

AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions
Topic 5.3: The Industrial Revolution Begins
GGreen DayFriday, December 4 SSilver DayMonday, December 7

OVERVIEW

Even before Paris argued about rights, a different revolution had begun in Britain: a change in how things were made. Today you find out why it began there. Nature gave Britain coal, iron, and water close together, and a shortage of wood that pushed it to coal. People built the rest: better farms, growing towns, laws that protected property, cotton from abroad, and money to invest. Then you see what the factory changed: it put the work in one place and gave each worker one small job.

REQUIRED WORK

Today you are responsible only for the modules listed under Required Work. You are welcome to use the other BeHistorical modules for review, support, or enrichment, but they are not required unless your teacher tells you otherwise.

  • 02 First & 10 Reading. First & 10: Coal, Water, and One Roof, plus all three check questions inside the reading.
  • 05 AP Skill Builder. Explain a Process, Step by Step.
  • 06 Checkpoint 1. Two things nature gave Britain and two things people built, what each made cheaper or possible, and how two of them worked together.
  • 10 Checkpoint 2. How the factory gathered production in one place, how it split the work into specialized jobs, and why that made more goods.

OPTIONAL SUPPORT / GO DEEPER
  • 01 Map & Geography Check.
  • 03 Content Delivery.
  • 04 BeSurreal. Cromford, Derbyshire, 1772.
  • 07 Evidence Lab. Choose at least two evidence cards. For each, say what kind of source it is and who made it, name one precise detail rather than summarizing it, explain what that detail shows about a cause of industrialization or about the factory system, and name one thing the source cannot tell you. The caption identifies the source; it does not supply your conclusion.
  • 08 Primary Source. Adam Smith and Andrew Ure on Dividing the Work.
  • 09 BeInTheRoom. Nottingham, early 1771. At Richard Arkwright's partners' table, decide where to build the new spinning mill, how to divide the work inside it, and how to pay for it and protect it.

These resources are available if you need more explanation, practice, or review. Gather All My Work collects every box on the page, so these will come through empty if you skip them. That is expected, not a mistake.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how Britain's environment (its coal, iron, and timber, and its rivers, coast, and canals) and the things people built (better farming, growing towns, laws that protected property, resources from abroad, and saved-up capital) worked together to cause industrial production to grow, starting in Britain.
  • I can explain how the factory system gathered production in a single place and split the work into specialized jobs, and why that let a mill make more goods.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain two things nature gave Britain (such as coal and iron, the shortage of wood, or rivers, the coast, and canals) and two things people built (such as better farming, towns, patents, cotton from abroad, or saved-up money). For each one, I can say what it made cheaper or possible. I can show one way two of them worked together.
  • I can describe the putting-out system, explain how a mill like Arkwright's at Cromford (1771) brought workers to water-powered machines in one building, explain how the work in a cotton mill was split into steps (carding, drawing, roving, and spinning) with each worker tending one, use Adam Smith's pin workshop (1776) to explain why splitting the work made more goods, and connect the factory to one environmental factor, such as the water that turned its wheel.
